extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and worldbuilders designing magic systems (especially fantasy authors, YA/middle-grade writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for creating effective magic systems in fiction, covering hard vs. soft systems, audience considerations, thematic/social implications, and techniques for making magic feel satisfying and meaningful in story. Emphasizes both practical craft choices and examples from published works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard vs. soft distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard = rules, crunchy. Soft = more free-form, less description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the system is rule-driven (hard) or mysterious/ambiguous (soft). Hard systems expose rules that create puzzles and constraints; soft systems provide flavor and feeling without explicit mechanics. The episode explicitly notes both are valid and will be discussed in separate episodes; choosing one affects how the story uses magic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/audience appropriateness for system rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: With younger readers, you can get away with a softer magic system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For middle-grade and younger audiences, less explicit rule-detail is acceptable; wonder and mystery can be more valuable than crunchy mechanics. Example: The Third Eye uses a softer system drawing on mythology tailored to a younger audience. Adjust the amount of exposition and complexity to reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw from mythology/folklore and craft to fit story
rubrics_metrics.description: Take something from mythology or folklore, and turn it into a system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mining myth/folklore (e.g., Shiva's third eye, Ganesh's mouse) provides resonant imagery and ready-made motifs; adapt or change elements to fit your narrative needs rather than copying wholesale. Use familiar archetypes as scaffolding, then craft rules, limits, or flavor that serve plot and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wish fulfillment / aspirational geewhiz
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are often looking for magic that is fun and aspirational — 'I want to do that' feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design powers and scenes that inspire reader desire (Hogwarts, cool spells). Balancing aspirational fun with meaningful cost or social consequences can deepen interest. Make some magic inherently appealing so readers experience escapism positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escapism balanced with relatable conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers want escapism — a world of new experiences — but where they can still identify with the problems and conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While crafting wondrous settings, ensure characters face relatable stakes and emotional problems so readers can connect. Use magic to amplify interpersonal and moral dilemmas rather than replace them with spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative/social exploration / thematic implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the flipside: how will new rules change people and relationships? Use magic to ask 'what if' social/speculative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the magic system as a tool for social commentary or to explore power dynamics (examples: Steelheart mapping absolute power; Runelords' social inequality). Think through societal effects and incorporate them into plot, institutions, and daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magic as puzzle — rules producing satisfying problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic systems can be 'giant puzzles' where you know the pieces and enjoy figuring how they solve the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For hard systems, reveal constraints and abilities in ways that let attentive readers anticipate solutions. Use 'plot coupons' — set up elements early that pay off later. Example: Mistborn's engineered puzzle-like uses of abilities. Avoid deus ex machina by foreshadowing and consistent rule application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual/sensory component to magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic should have a visual component — make it look and feel tangible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even mental or conceptual powers benefit from visual cues (e.g., Mistborn's blue lines). Sensory detail helps readers imagine using the magic and grounds abstract systems. Add visual markers, textures, or signals that convey mechanics and emotional tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising yet inevitable payoff (fulfilling promises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good magic is surprising but its consequences feel inevitable; it fulfills the promises set up earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules and foreshadowing so that climactic uses of magic feel earned and inevitable while still surprising the reader. The 'surprising, yet inevitable' quality is illustrated by examples like Deadbeat's necromancy scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-through on ramifications / show societal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow through on the ramifications of the magic; show how society is shaped by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't merely present a conceit — explore its consequences across institutions, relationships, economics, and culture. Authors like Runelords and Mistborn are cited as handling ramifications well. This deepens realism and thematic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety — don't force every system into one mold
rubrics_metrics.description: There needs to be variety; not every magic system has to be puzzle-based or share the same traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different strengths of hard vs soft approaches and tonal choices. Use different traditions (high magic, low magic, urban fantasy) appropriately; readers expect diversity across works and subgenres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits, costs, and sacrifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic that requires sacrifice or causes pain can be powerful; limits and costs make magic meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce trade-offs (sacrifice, diminishing returns, vulnerable sources) to prevent magic from becoming an all-purpose solution and to raise stakes. Balance 'wish fulfillment' against believable costs to maintain tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with character growth and stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: How magic ties into character arcs: remove support systems so characters must rely on themselves and the magic in meaningful ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use magic as part of the protagonist's growth (e.g., The Third Eye removes supports so protagonist must rely on herself and soft magic). Make magic decisions reflect character choices and development; ensure magic usage has emotional and narrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency / rules and their application (Sanderson's Laws implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up rules or laws for the magic and apply them consistently; if you explain it, use it as a logical system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether explicitly invoking 'Sanderson's Laws' or not, maintain internal logic for hard systems; identify loopholes intentionally and address them. For soft systems, maintain a consistent 'flavor' so the reader intuitively understands limits even without a mechanics list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct flavor or experiential feel for soft magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft magic systems may not state rules but should convey a distinct flavor — you know what it's like to experience that magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without formal mechanics, give readers a reliable sense of how magic behaves emotionally and experientially (Prydain example). Use evocative language and recurring motifs so the magic's presence is coherent and satisfying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and content suitability (graphic/gruesome elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of tone and audience sensitivity — gruesome scenes may delight target readers and upset gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauge graphic content for your intended audience (example: middle-grade readers enjoying gruesome scenes while parents complained). Align visceral detail, horror elements, and tonal choices with age-appropriateness and marketing expectations.
